query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coatings, creep resistance is achieved because stable FCC/BCC phase boundaries create localized elastic strain fields from lattice distortion, which impede continuous dislocation glide (including non-Schmid slip) and delay shear band formation under sustained loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating comprising a dual-phase microstructure with an FCC matrix interspersed by BCC regions that form coherent or semi-coherent phase boundaries with controlled lattice misfit.
generation.intervention: Subject the coating to continuous high-temperature/high-stress loading while performing a controlled comparison with a compositionally modified variant where the FCC/BCC phase boundaries are intentionally disrupted (i.e., higher lattice misfit) or otherwise less stable.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted within the normal operational temperature and stress ranges of the coating system, ensuring that processing history and microstructure (except for the phase boundary characteristics) are kept equivalent.
generation.structural_mediator: The FCC/BCC phase boundaries that generate localized elastic strain fields due to lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: Under load, these stable phase boundaries act as barriers to dislocation glide and help promote non-Schmid slip behavior, thereby dispersing strain and preventing the localization of plastic deformation that typically leads to shear band development. Altering these boundaries (by increasing the lattice misfit) would reduce this barrier effect and accelerate creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under sustained stress, the baseline coating with optimal, stable phase boundaries is predicted to show lower creep strain rates and fewer/smaller shear bands compared to the variant with altered (less stable) phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: The unmodified coating with well-optimized, minimally misfitting FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under the normal service conditions of the coating (i.e., within a temperature and stress range that maintains phase interfacial integrity); conditions that cause phase decomposition or excessive coarsening would lie outside these boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: Although the qualitative role of phase boundary stability is supported by prior microstructural observations, the precise quantitative effect on creep strain rate and dislocation dynamics remains to be established through systematic experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two series of protective coatings: one with the baseline optimized FCC/BCC phase boundaries and one with intentionally altered phase boundary characteristics (e.g., increased lattice misfit via compositional modifications). Subject both series to identical continuous high-temperature and high-stress loading while monitoring creep deformation. Use electron microscopy and diffraction techniques to track dislocation activity and shear band formation.
measurements: microstructural evolution (dislocation density, shear band density)
phase boundary character (via TEM/SEM imaging and diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating with altered phase boundaries demonstrates comparable creep resistance (i.e., similar creep strain rates and similar microstructural stability) to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis that stable FCC/BCC phase boundaries are the governing factor for creep resistance would be falsified.

Coarse slip bands and non-Schmid’s translational slip lead to shear bands formation in body-centered cubic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe microstructural evolution and shear band formation mechanism in an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr body-centered cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloy (HEA) were systematically investigated during cold rolling. Microstructural observations revealed the development of coarse, and straight slip bands at early deformation stages. Detailed analysis of slip band–grain boundary (GB) interactions showed evidence of continuous slip transmission across GB regions. With increasing deformation, localized strain regions evolved along the prior slip bands, eventually leading to the formation of well-defined shear bands. Non-Schmid effects were found to promote slip continuity across GBs, preferentially along the {112} slip planes, thereby facilitating strain localization. Creep Behavior and Its Influencing Factors in High-Entropy Superalloys: A Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study

Abstract: AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Small-Scale Insight into Uniform Deformability and Softening Resistance of Refractory High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Owing to the outstanding softening resistance and thermal stability of BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs), their unique deformation-induced defect structures merit investigation. Therefore, this study evaluated the mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of W-based low- to high-entropy alloys at various temperatures and orientations using nanoindentation and microcompression, complemented by post-mortem TEM and atomistic simulations to observe dislocation populations and their evolution. Results reveal that HEAs exhibit reduced elastic and plastic anisotropy while retaining high-temperature strength. With increasing compositional complexity, planar slip and abrupt stress drops were progressively replaced by homogeneous flow and smoother serrations. Severe lattice distortion promoted dislocation nucleation but impeded long-range glide, enabling cooperative edge and screw dislocation activity that sustained strength and work hardening across temperatures.
